Will a power station run my gas furnace?

Scenarios Updated 2026-08-08

The gas does the heating; what needs electricity is the circulating blower and the control board, and a US Department of Energy field study puts that at 422–548 W depending on which motor is in the cabinet. That is a few hundred watts rather than a few thousand, and it is why a furnace is the best-value load in a winter outage. It is also why this site will not hand you a green light: of the 12 published US machines here, 11 come out marginal and 1 refuses outright.

What caps those rows is a missing number rather than a failed test. The figure it is waiting on is the locked-rotor current of a direct-drive blower motor, and we went looking for it three separate times — through manufacturer motor catalogues and original-equipment electrical data tables — without finding one. On every table we opened that carries a locked-rotor column at all, that column belongs to the compressor.

A few hundred watts, and which motor decides it

What a furnace asks of a battery

The two running figures come from one federal field study of furnace blower motors. The empty rows are empty on purpose, and each carries the date the search behind it was last run.

Older split-capacitor blower — heating mode 548 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · medium confidence

The conventional permanent split-capacitor motor still in most cabinets more than a few years old.

Run this pairing →
Brushless variable-speed blower — heating mode 422 W Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · medium confidence

The same study measured the brushless permanent-magnet motors using 126 W — twenty-three per cent — less in heating mode. In circulation-only mode the gap is far larger, and so is the drop in airflow.

Locked-rotor current of that motor Not found in the sources we checked no figure to date

The figure a surge verdict would be computed from. Three rounds of searching are recorded on this field, naming the catalogues and data sheets that were opened.

Minimum circuit ampacity, from the furnace maker 1,702 VA Official spec · verified 2026-08-01 · medium confidence

A furnace manufacturer’s stated circuit requirement at 115 V, with a band across the range from 943 to 1,760 VA. It describes a conductor, not a running draw.

Official spec · verified 2026-08-02 · gas furnace blower record · DOE field study + manufacturer spec sheets

The number that is there instead, and why it is not a surge figure

Furnace spec sheets carry minimum circuit ampacity, and the manufacturer prints the formula beside it: 1.25 times the circulator blower amperes, plus the inducer blower amperes. That 1.25 is the continuous-load factor from conductor sizing — it exists so a wire does not run warm for hours, and it says nothing about the first tenth of a second. Sizing a battery from it overshoots substantially, which is safe; multiplying it by a start-up factor to manufacture an inrush is neither safe nor meaningful, because it compounds one safety margin with another and prints the result as physics.

A furnace blower against the published US library, computed on this build

Note how little the load-ratio column explains here. A machine at fourteen per cent of continuous output lands in the same state as one at ninety-one per cent, because most of these rows are decided by a surge ceiling against a start-up demand nobody has stated — and our engine caps a motor load in that condition at marginal rather than passing it.

Where we looked, and what was there

Three rounds, recorded on the record with dates. A full-line blower motor catalogue and a major motor maker’s heating and cooling catalogue list direct-drive blower motors with an amperes column and no locked-rotor column at all. An air-handler technical guide lists full-load amperes, minimum circuit ampacity and maximum overcurrent protection, and nothing else. Two original-equipment furnace electrical data tables do carry a locked-rotor column — and it belongs to the compressor, with the blower row showing only full-load amperes and horsepower. Three rounds, three different kinds of document, one result: locked-rotor current declared for the compressor and absent for the direct-drive blower. That is why we treat this as a wall rather than as a gap in our own searching, and why the only route left to a figure here is measuring one.

Why this load has no record page of its own

Every other load in this article’s neighbourhood has a page at /appliances/. This one has no page at all, and the record’s own publish gate names the reason in one line: a motor load with no surge source would let the compatibility check wave through a machine that cannot actually start it. So the figures stay quotable and the page stays unbuilt. That is the same decision as the marginal cap above, taken one layer down — and it is why the links here go to the calculator rather than to a record page.

The part we are not going to tell you

How to connect it. The furnace maker’s own sheet states 115 VAC, 60 Hz, single phase, with overcurrent protection of 15–20 A, and every path from a battery to a furnace runs through fixed wiring. That is a licensed electrician’s work with a transfer arrangement, and this site publishes load parameters rather than wiring methods. Our records also carry no waveform requirement for this load, so our engine runs no waveform test on it.

Questions people ask

Will a power station run a gas furnace?
Very likely in electrical terms, and this library will not confirm it. A federal field study puts a furnace blower at 422 W to 548 W in heating mode, which most mid-size machines carry comfortably on running watts. But no machine here earns a green verdict: eleven of twelve come out marginal and one refuses, because a motor load with no stated start-up current is capped at marginal by our engine rather than passed.
How many watts does a furnace blower use?
Between 422 W and 548 W in heating mode, and which end you get is set by the motor rather than the furnace. A US Department of Energy field study measured brushless permanent-magnet motors using 126 W — twenty-three per cent — less than conventional split-capacitor motors doing the same job. The figure on the furnace spec sheet is usually minimum circuit ampacity instead, which is a wiring requirement and runs far higher.
Why is every machine on this page marginal rather than a pass?
Because the start-up demand is unknown, and our engine will not treat unknown as harmless for a motor. Direct-drive furnace blower motors are listed with an amperes column and no locked-rotor column, in a full-line motor catalogue, a major maker’s heating and cooling catalogue and an air-handler technical guide alike; the original-equipment tables that do carry locked-rotor current carry it for the compressor instead. Until that figure is measured, a green verdict here would be an assertion rather than a calculation.
